title: Lincoln Waits for a Victory
text:
By the summer of 1862 Abraham Lincoln had decided to declare the freedom of slaves in the states in rebellion. On 22 July he read a draft of the proclamation to his cabinet. He made clear that he had made up his mind on the policy and wanted advice only on details.

Secretary of State William Seward raised an objection about timing. The Union army had just suffered a string of defeats in Virginia. Lincoln later told the painter Francis Carpenter what Seward had argued: that issued at such a moment, the proclamation might be seen as the act of an exhausted government, a cry for help, or, in Lincoln's recollection of Seward's phrase, as "our last shriek, on the retreat". Better to wait and issue it on the back of a military success. Lincoln said the argument struck him with great force, and he put the draft away.

The wait was longer than he hoped. In August the Union lost again at the Second Battle of Bull Run. Then, on 17 September 1862, Union forces stopped Robert E. Lee's invasion of Maryland at Antietam. It was not a crushing victory, but it was enough. Five days later Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, and the final proclamation took effect on 1 January 1863. The new war aim made it much harder for Britain and France to support the Confederacy.
lesson: The same message can read as strength or desperation depending on when it arrives. Choose your moment so that a bold decision looks like confidence.
source: Francis B. Carpenter, Six Months at the White House with Abraham Lincoln (1866); Doris Kearns Goodwin, Team of Rivals (2005)
